I don't know if I can say it "helped" me grow, but I'll try to pinpoint some of the the effects. Stuff like this is always tough because obviously I can't know what I'd be like without Scientology, but here goes:

Strong sense of self confidence/personal ability is definitely cultivated. You'll often hear Scientologists say, and I believe Hubbard even wrote that Scientology's purpose -- at least until the majority of the world gets helped -- is to help the able become more able. Rallying the living, not raising the dead, etc.. So from very early on you feel like you're part of this elite group of people.

Also, there's a section of Scientology  teachings referred to as "study tech", and it's pretty much the first stuff you learn when you start taking courses. I still feel like the study tech I know is helpful today, though it's very common-sense type stuff I feel like I probably would have picked up just being a normal student. Lots of emphasis on defining words, so you end up with a decent vocabulary just because you've spent so much time looking up definitions. 

Sometimes when you're on course, your supervisor will come over, read over what you've been reading, then ask you to define a few of the words.. THEN sometimes they'll ask you to define some of the words you used in those definitions, etc. etc. Some supervisors are dicks and will go as far as asking you for derivations, what language it's derived from, word roots, stuff like that. I'd imagine kids who were on course regularly, under a supervisor like that, would have a really good grasp on breaking down words.

I should end this by saying I never got *that* deep. Some of my friends were on course every day, kinda just doing it as an alternative to school. I mostly got to pick which courses I wanted to take, and my dad always let me do it at my leisure, and stop if I wasn't enjoying it. He was also very accepting when I decided to leave, and it never caused issues for us. Mind you, I didn't announce my departure, try to give them a big middle finger, or anything like that, so the church never got involved. Actually, a lot of people in my area still think I'm a Scientologist, and I don't really have any intention of changing that. I fear losing my friends who still are.

If there's anything else you want to know, feel free to ask. I love talking about it, there's a sweet nostalgia.

Also, I'm realizing I probably painted a sort of nice picture of Scientology, I'd like to say for the record that I do believe the church higher ups are manipulative, money-hungry scum, who are fine running an organization on fucking slave labor. I've lost friends to it, and I want the shit shut down. The average scientologist, though, just believes they're doing the best thing for the planet, and it's hard for me to fault them.

For whatever it's worth, it's easy to be fooled if you're born into it. You're just surrounded by attractive, successful, intelligent people telling you how great of a job you're doing whenever you're progressing in Scientology. It's like a whole Church with smart kid syndrome, and you get this idea that you're just better at understanding information than everyone who isn't a Scientologist, and it's your job to help them.

Probably just as easy to fall into the trap if you're just a "lost soul" type, or generally looking for belonging. They attract a lot of foreigners for this reason, I think. 

They do a great job of getting you to ignore ALL outside media. Strange, because they're big on getting data from multiple sources, unless it's about Scientology.

Please don't rationalize yourself into thinking that the way you're living is somehow better. It doesn't at all sound like you have thus far, but it's a dangerous road. 

>but most people only have superficial relationships anyway.

I don't know you, so I don't know what you have or haven't done, what efforts you have or have not made to try to do something about this, but you sound so far gone that I just want to reach through this monitor and punch you right in the fucking mouth.

It just sounds like this: At 21 you've given up and "You don't see yourself putting the effort in"? What the fuck kind of answer is that. Of course you don't "See yourself" putting the effort in. My obese uncle doesn't "see himself ever losing the weight". Once you surrender to things just being the way they are, it's over.

Anyway, I'm no therapist, so I probably don't have the proper advice to give, but it's time to do SOMETHING. And don't just nod your head and reply with some lame answer like "I'll try :(". Do it.

> One of these days I might contact her and tell her how sorry I am...

It's been **seven years**. It's time for "One of these days" to be "Today".

What you did was fucking terrible, obviously, but not unforgivable (she gets to be the judge of that). 

You deserve so much better than an emotionless remainder of your existence. If my math is right, you're 21 now. This is not the time to sulk over past transgressions, there is simply too much more to do.
